summary: An ESP32-C5 expansion board for the Flipper Zero, notable mainly because the C5 is Espressif's first dual-band part, so this is one of the few Flipper add-ons that can actually see and attack 5 GHz Wi-Fi. It also carries a high-output 940 nm IR blaster, an OLED status screen and a microSD slot, and can be driven either from the Flipper over UART or standalone over USB-C.
honest_take: The genuinely new thing here is the ESP32-C5's 5 GHz radio; the rest is a well-built carrier board for firmware someone else writes for free. At ~$146 you are paying roughly ten times the cost of a bare ESP32-C5 dev board for the Flipper form factor, the IR section and Rabbit-Labs' QC. Also note that deauth on 5 GHz is increasingly a dead end: any network with 802.11w/PMF enabled (mandatory on WPA3, common on modern WPA2 gear) simply ignores the frames.

summary: A passive infrared LED array that plugs onto the Flipper Zero's GPIO header and replaces the Flipper's single weak IR LED with a wide-angle flood of high-output 940 nm emitters. It is a range-and-coverage upgrade for the Flipper's existing Infrared app: universal-remote work, TV-B-Gone style sweeps, and hitting several devices in a room at once.
honest_take: Two things to be clear about. First, this is a resistor-and-LED board with no chip on it - $60-$86 buys you Rabbit-Labs' thermal design, hand assembly and the credit-card-slim form factor, not silicon. Second, the IR flood is for consumer remote-control protocols, not for blinding security cameras: these LEDs emit 38 kHz-modulated pulse trains a few milliseconds long, most surveillance cameras run an IR-cut filter in daylight and auto-exposure at night, and even if you did bloom the sensor you would produce an obvious white glare that reads as deliberate tampering. Treat 'IR flood' as 'wider remote coverage', not as camera defeat.

name: Rabbit-Labs Flux Capacitor (Amplified CC1101)
firmware: n/a - uses the Flipper's external sub-GHz module support
firmware_note: No firmware of its own. The Flipper drives it over hardware SPI once Sub-GHz > Radio Settings is switched from Internal to External; Momentum and Unleashed builds also drive the PA enable lines.
price_note: 58.99 with the stock 433 MHz antenna, 63.99 with the high-gain antenna. Checked 2026-09-06, in stock. The Ebyte E07-433M20S module it is built around costs roughly $8-12 on its own.
skill_note: Physically plug-and-play, but you must switch the Flipper to the external radio, and you must understand that an amplified TX has legal consequences the internal radio does not.
build_note: Accessory: requires a Flipper Zero (GPIO header). An antenna MUST be attached before transmitting or the PA can be damaged.
summary: A Flipper Zero GPIO board carrying an Ebyte E07-433M20S module - a CC1101 with an integrated power amplifier and low-noise amplifier - on a low-noise 5 V regulated supply with an SMA antenna. It replaces the Flipper's internal sub-GHz radio for both receive and transmit, raising rated TX from the CC1101's +12 dBm maximum to +20 dBm and adding an LNA on receive.
honest_take: Two hard truths. One: the amplifier is band-locked. The E07-433M20S is specified 425-450.5 MHz, so this board is a 433 MHz device - at 315 MHz, 868 MHz or 915 MHz the PA and matching network are out of band and you are worse off than the Flipper's stock radio, not better. Two: the extra power is the legally dangerous part. In the US, 433 MHz consumer remotes operate under FCC Part 15.231, which caps field strength at roughly 11 mV/m at 3 m and forbids continuous transmission; +20 dBm into a gain antenna is far outside that, and 433.05-434.79 MHz overlaps the 70 cm amateur band, where unlicensed transmission is separately prohibited. Ten dB is also only about 3x the range in free space, not the kilometres the module's marketing implies - that figure assumes 5 dBi antennas at 2.5 m height in open ground at 1.2 kbps, not a jammer-in-a-pocket scenario.

summary: A credit-card-thin PCB carrying an H-bridge, two large capacitors and a coil, based on Samy Kamkar's MagSpoof. Attached to a Flipper Zero it generates a changing magnetic field that a magnetic-stripe reader head interprets as a card being swiped, letting you replay previously captured track data. Its practical selling point over the Flipper's internal-TX hack is that it does not risk damaging the Flipper's own radio hardware.
honest_take: This is a legacy attack that gets less useful every year, and the board cannot read anything - it only replays track data you already have, in a format you had to obtain some other way. Against modern payment it is essentially dead: EMV chip and contactless generate a per-transaction cryptogram, so a cloned magstripe fails, and US merchants have been chip-liable since 2015. Where it still works is old, dumb readers - hotel door locks, gym and arcade cards, some parking and access badges, and time clocks - which is genuinely a real physical-red-team niche, just a much narrower one than the word 'MagSpoof' suggests. Also budget for frustration: the app the vendor points you at is openly described as buggy, and upstream magspoof_flipper has not had a code push since April 2025.

honest_take: It is not an ESP32 board and comparing it to one misses the point - it is a 2014-era Android tablet SoC running Debian, which is both its strength (real aircrack-ng, real drivers, real scripting) and its weakness (512 MB RAM, a slow A7 cluster, and Wi-Fi that depends on Realtek out-of-tree drivers being happy). The 5 GHz capability everyone quotes comes from the bundled RTL8821CU USB dongle, not from the board's own RTL8723DS radio. Supply is the real problem: it sells out constantly, and the creator's hardware licence (CC BY-NC-SA) explicitly asks people not to resell boards, so there is no second source.

summary: The 'Big Flipper Board' from the author of ESP32 Marauder: a maximalist Flipper add-on carrying an ESP32-C5 for dual-band Wi-Fi, two separate CC1101 radios individually tuned for the 400 MHz and 900 MHz bands, an nRF24 with PA and LNA, GPS and a microSD slot, with five SMA connectors on the edge. honest_take: The two band-tuned CC1101s are the genuinely clever bit - a single CC1101 with one antenna is always a compromise across 300-900 MHz, and splitting it lets you also hang your own amplifier on each band. Everything else is the usual multiboard bill of materials, just done properly. name: nRF24L01+ module for Flipper Zero (mousejack / 2.4 GHz)
firmware: n/a - driven by Flipper apps over SPI
firmware_note: The module has no firmware. Flipper apps talk to it directly over SPI: mothball187's nrf24 suite (sniffer and mousejacker), vad7's nrf24scan and nRF24-Batch, and several community jammer apps.
vendor: Generic - Nordic Semiconductor silicon on modules from countless Chinese board houses; also sold pre-wired by Flipper accessory shops
price_note: A bare nRF24L01+ module is roughly 2-5 USD; the PA+LNA version with an SMA antenna is roughly 6-12 USD. Pre-assembled Flipper-format boards with an nRF24 on them run 15-70 USD. Estimated from typical marketplace pricing rather than a single vendor page.
skill_note: Buying the module is trivial; wiring seven SPI lines to the right Flipper GPIO pins, and understanding that most of the famous attacks no longer land, is the real work.
build_note: Accessory: requires a Flipper Zero. A bare module needs jumper wires or soldering to the GPIO header (2, 3, 4, 5, plus 3.3V and GND on the usual mapping); the Flipper's 'Extra 7' GPIO preset in Momentum and Unleashed exists for exactly this. Multiboards fit the same chip pre-wired.
summary: A Nordic nRF24L01+ transceiver on a small module, wired to the Flipper's GPIO header. It gives the Flipper access to the 2.4 GHz band outside Wi-Fi and Bluetooth: scanning for proprietary GFSK links, sniffing and replaying wireless keyboard and mouse traffic, and the MouseJack keystroke-injection attack. It is by far the cheapest capability upgrade a Flipper can get.
honest_take: Two blunt points. First, MouseJack is a 2016 vulnerability. Bastille disclosed it in February 2016, the vendors shipped receiver firmware updates that year, mousejack.com is now a dead link, and the canonical Flipper app (mothball187's) has had no code push since August 2022 - so treat 'it can hijack wireless keyboards' as 'it might, against a ten-year-old unpatched dongle you find in a drawer'. Second, the 'nRF24 jammer' apps that make this module popular are not jammers in any meaningful sense: the chip is a narrowband GFSK transceiver with 1 MHz channels and 0 dBm output, so what those apps do is hop a single tone around, which can disrupt other nRF24-family links on the same channels and will do essentially nothing to Wi-Fi or to a connected Bluetooth link. Nordic themselves list the whole nRF24 series as not recommended for new designs, which tells you where this technology sits.
